translations.title: Pause, learned Jáuregui, your proud course
translations.text:
Pause, learned Jáuregui, your proud course

of the brush that deals out eternity,

when Nature, when art,

yield to breathing linen, living metal.


I do not set down your symmetrical marvels,

for even the least will know how to immortalize you;

nor describe you in the more heroic part

where you wrest from the sun its elusive laurel.


Lay down the numbers, or the colors: the brush describes,

the pen paints,

and each pours out what seemed impossible.


Let your applause not hinder your wonders: to heap

such a sum of astonishments

is an impossible burden for fame.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Prodigious Mendoza, whom fame can never praise too much
translations.text:
Prodigious Mendoza, whom fame can never praise too much,

though in all things it is wholly yours;

your wise, perhaps Gothic, lineage

is crowned by the sun with its virgin branch.


How fiercely the sun burns! Does it shine, or love?

Even death itself is unsettled by it.

If it prunes the whole tree of life,

what good is its fiery axe?


So many mortals breathe their last

that, dead, I see the same number still.

All earth is tomb now, no longer shelter.


Are these punishments, my God, or signs?

If signs, leave some alive as an example—

lives, all of which die by punishment.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Your stubborn corpse warns us
translations.text:
Your stubborn corpse warns us

that life may be dead, yet not defeated,

for only in your courage, only in your life,

did death behold something beyond itself.


Fate is strong, but you were stronger:

your fall was not owed to its blow;

you helped it, once it was overcome—

who but you could conquer you?


You divided the indivisible passage

between dying and falling, so proud

that common ruin finds no parallel in you.


How much more than immortal, than invincible,

I shall deem you, when alive,

now that I gaze on your fearless corpse!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Raise up your divine Zion, Lord
translations.text:
Raise up your divine Zion, Lord,

where, ungrateful for so great a gift,

the Godhead made man a sacrifice,

and, struck down, he struck it down.


Let the wanderer's ambition not attain its guilt

in this sign, though prostrate;

let the sacrilegious purpose of his trade

not make a temple's memory of the ruin.


Unless, coveting the outrage,

fearing that violence has ended,

that it gave impiety its final sign—


(while it does not provoke you to fresh fury,

lest patience stand idle)—

you too would suffer to see yourself without a temple.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Noble city, crowned with kings
translations.text:
Noble city, crowned with kings,

steadfast in the clear light of two fortunes: first

through glories filled with waning moons,

then illumined by Gothic suns.


From today I see both swords

become one in the hands of time,

and overcome the stubborn powers

of unconquered oblivion and envy.


May the sun acclaim you, steadfast and famed,

wherever sand is kissed and foam is licked,

for today the finest swan has sung to you.


O Granada, victorious in two lights!

Your fame flies on such a lofty wing;

steadfast, you stand upon the highest height.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Happy am I, if I temper my dreams
translations.text:
Happy am I, if I temper my dreams

as they rush toward this precipice.

Yesterday it was a temple; today, its trace.

Where can I flee, if the temple suffers?


Just, though adverse, I behold you, Jove,

if warning comes before the punishment,

and less vengeful than kind

if I learn from you what I await.


Yet, Father of Heaven, whatever lies

lofty within your vast, ordained power

accuses your harshness, as its creator.


Does what is born exalted somehow sin?

Is greatness itself a crime? If so,

Jove, strike down Nature!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The voice to Italy, its echo to Spain
translations.text:
The voice to Italy, its echo to Spain,

the sacred swan I revere entrusts.

We doubt where it first was heard,

for echo is a voice and deceives like one.


Urbano's marvel today is not that he is welcomed

by the whole world, nor do I praise him for being great;

what I praise is his power to grow

in his greatest deed.


And you, Gabriel, who carry the harmony

of Tiber's king across my fields,

sing, in your labor, greater than Orpheus.


Orpheus was praised for stilling waves,

not for mingling rivers;

you joined Tiber to Tagus.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Lord, that I might see frozen flint...
translations.text:
Lord, that I might see frozen flint

bleed fiery blood from wounded steel!

That hardened bronze should steal obedience

from wax, warmed by heat!


That a mountain tremble at a feared lightning bolt,

while man, struck by it, feels nothing!

For, if you consider it, each sin within the sinner

is lightning without a sound.


What villain, with a merciless viper

settled on his breast while he slept,

would not awake and flee its venom?


Flee swiftly, O guilty plant!

Flee, for from this day's lightning

permission may turn to late thunder.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Lord, I am so deeply in your debt
translations.text:
Lord, I am so deeply in your debt

whenever thought allows me to reflect,

that though you have borne with me forever,

you show a patience that seems forgetful.


I, roused from sleep by your voice,

wake now to the voice of my sin;

and at the first pain of seeing it written,

you grant it the privilege of erasure.


It is debt, Lord, not trust,

to think this sacrifice of pain

may rise as pleasing fragrance to you.


Still you leave me hope, without a doubt: whoever

turns offense into a gift—what merit

can the very offering earn?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Who is it, illustrious Gaspar, who dies...
translations.text:
Who dies, illustrious Gaspar: you

in grief, or your ill-fated brother?

He did not die, since in a phantom form

your pale memory offers him to us;


You did not die, for in your dawn

the light of a sun that set too soon still shines.

How much what endures in man deceives,

since what is born must perish of its birth!


Happy is he who lives by fame,

not years, and takes this counsel: we breathe

in order to become immortal.


O envy (though it is called pity),

to mourn the one we miss because he ceases

to be what we mourn him for!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Then I live, because I die, when
translations.text:
Then I live, because I die, when

love teaches me to die more, while living;

for dying is no pain—it is life, when there is

a dying that is prepared, never complete.


Love seeks to die, finding a gentle

end that cannot be an end; and, perishing,

it builds more life, since birth alone

immortalizes nothing—only loving does.


In this spun labyrinth, then,

both judge and actor in my life,

in its last hour I teach it to be first.


Dead, yes, they will see me, but unchanged;

my death will give me back who I was, though gone,

if at last my being was then to be no more.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: That rare token of friendship
translations.text:
That rare token of friendship,

learned man of fire, Augustine's palace,

which proved more a mirror than a danger,

for it emerged clear from peril,


is a rebuke to greedy Aesculapius,

who, more than the fierce and malign humor,

denies the opposite crystal

and adds a defense to harshness itself.


If the accident should ever recur (God forbid!),

which inflames the body more than fear,

and you dread the element at your lips—


Since you are an eminent vessel of grace,

today you rub against the feared flame: ease

the fever, image of its injury.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Pain grows, and in proportion to its growth
translations.text:
Pain grows, and in proportion to its growth

the same ill lends me strength to bear it.

Who has ever seen endurance

turn into a kind of torment?


Habit, born of long suffering,

has made violence seem natural;

now only the absence of pain threatens me,

after pain has served me as food.


I despair of waiting for death,

since it is an ill that lasts so briefly

(though life barely keeps me standing).


Love's caution against my fate was this: to wound

my heart until it lost its wits,

so that afterward I would adore its pains.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: This dying, this final fate
translations.text:
This dying, this final fate

is the image of fear repeated,

and as an image so dreaded,

imagination makes it strong.


When, then, does dying happen, to be precise?

As we breathe our last? No, life remains.

When the soul has already parted?

That is already being dead, not dying.


Could dying be that instant

of the final breath? That point

where the last sigh turns into stillness?


No, for every point is alike

to certain life or being dead.

So when is dying? When we sin.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: What are jealousy’s? The greatest torment...
translations.text:
What are jealousies? The greatest torment: a viper

that feeds on the poison with which it kills others;

a hell that tortures memory, judgment,

and thought.


To admit chimeras, embrace the wind,

take the side of one's own disgrace;

seek to cure a sickness with what worsens it,

refuse experience its lesson.


To trust the slightest hint that calls,

though it distorts the judgment;

a flash without light, a fire without flame.


If jealousy is this, though mere chimera,

what will disillusion be? Woe to the lover!

Woe for the next time awaiting here!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The water gave the sought grave
translations.text:
The water gave the sought grave

—no longer a guest of fable—to Narcissus.

He who wished to imitate his bright death

possessed courage as his beauty.


Fortunate was his death, for it seeks

to turn a passion into a warning;

yet one who reaches the appointed end

may be unlucky in his good fortune.


Heaven endured the ardor of both,

either because it sprang from ignorance

or to restrain a third attempt.


Don Antonio did not die: he had died

already, having wasted a lesson.

What, then, died in the waters? His daring.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: As in a chamber of fine marble
translations.text:
As in a chamber whose floor

is fine marble, an idle boy,

with nimble hand and spirited gesture,

whips a little rounded top;


while he sees its circling course

last in the sphere his fury struck,

he pauses; seeing it come to rest,

he strikes again the sounding linen.


So Love, with harsh violence,

in the shifting realm of my care,

makes a game of wounding my heart.


And though pain's diligence is more than enough,

when it sees me quiet, laid low,

it is offended by that quiet.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Today, upon your faithless arm, elusive Hebrew
translations.text:
Today, upon your faithless arm, elusive Hebrew,

God lies once more—not as before,

a divine phoenix reborn alive

in fierce fire from lofty ashes.


Today reason calls us to his love,

for he died so true a lover

that, since Love became his heir,

he binds himself to us in successive fire.


If this wondrous holocaust demands

wings that in swift flight bring earth

news of so profound a mystery,


They are not lacking: at your prodigious call,

unmatched Soria, a phoenix entrusts

its flight to you; Arabia is its world.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: How long will this dye, tell me, Fabio
translations.text:
How long, tell me, Fabio, will this dye

set your deceit upon your head?

He who makes treachery his nature

should fear time's perfidious harm.


Since, then, with little wisdom

you insult the years' purity,

dye your wrinkles too; it is base

that cheek and lip should look so different.


A lie in speech is shameful;

without pretext or excuse,

it is a crime that stains one's honor.


Oh Fabio, how much more I see you sin,

taking this guilt so very seriously

that you get away with lying in silence!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Great are the eyes, brief the sight
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: It cannot be; feeling lies
translations.text:
It cannot be; feeling lies,

for pain, blind, cannot testify,

or it suffers an exception, like an enemy

that offers the fight to endurance.


I fear a false thought from Phyllis,

and more when I fear it as punishment,

for perhaps I wake within myself

what Phyllis's intention still sleeps on.


To tell her not to fear her change

would make her think I distrust her;

I fear to feed my pain if I believe her.


Distrust, I want you to stay neutral: while

the feared event is still at hand,

be true only in my present moment.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Happy brute, you have won; now all bow
translations.text:
Happy brute, you have won; now all

creation inclines to become your living story.

Victory did not fit within your life;

you hid victory in ruin.


A death requiring divine force

had Jove's manifest divinity.

Philip did not strike: with greater glory,

he who dared await him deals the blow.


Desire made the shot; the hand

struck, when the beast, twice wounded,

saw its life mortal, its fate alive.


O mighty shot of a sovereign master!

The blow took away its life,

and its master took away its death.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: You have won, Phyllis
translations.text:
You have won, Phyllis. In my breast

the first tenderness takes root today;

like ice touched by the infant sun,

I weep, yet with rebellious, chilly courage.


My stubbornness wanes, not my free will;

this feeling to which fate brings me

arises as pleasure, not as law;

if I give it room, it will not rule.


Let reason reign, and my passions

be subject only to the law of vassals

within my inward, loving monarchy.


If love conspires against the laws of subjects

to stir them to rebellion,

I shall turn my empire to tyranny.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Jordan thought it heard a second time
translations.text:
Jordan thought it heard a second time

the voice of John, which you fulfilled;

despite the distance, it restrained

its cold current in equal wonder.


It could doubt, hearing you today,

and having heard John, who worked more: he

who then softened stones, or he

who now persuades hearts.


You so resemble the Jordan's swan

that heaven, to end the doubt,

dressed you in black plumes, jealously.


But song remained in doubt,

while you kept the praise that doubt bestowed,

your voice disproving those dark feathers.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Phyllis, whose fierce lover’s death
translations.text:
Phyllis, whose fierce lover's death

stole more soul than it left to his life,

and now honors her husband's mortal wound

in orphaned relics,


saw a portrait, a flattering likeness,

a false shadow of true love;

and when she let it bring her comfort,

she knew it was no true soul.


Scrupulous at finding herself distracted,

“Alas,” she said, “beloved lover, I dare not

look at your shade, lest I lose you.


I gave my whole soul so wholly to your death

that now I cannot feel anew,

not even the pain of not seeing you alive.”
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Not where the Tagus bathes golden plumes
translations.text:
Not where the Tagus bathes golden plumes,

pilgrim swan of Lusitania,

is he greater, dying as a god

when his final voice deceives the sea.


If a swan dies there, a Spanish swan

is born in pilgrim Don Álvaro,

who opens a road to immortality

with a new voice that gladdens and disillusions.


Changing tongues and feathers, he makes

his homeland doubtful: Spanish soil

contends with Latin and Lusitanian.


I, wishing to name his lovely homeland,

behold his sovereign spirit:

it can only be of heaven.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: I saw a laurel whose sacred disdain
translations.text:
I saw a laurel whose sacred disdain

Apollo could not overcome, so thick its boughs.

There Daphne still lived in disdain,

still forgiving Phoebus none of his devotion.


Why should my disillusioned love

turn deaf to experience each day,

if a god gives example to my stubbornness,

and what is dead lives on in what is adored?


Apollo loves Daphne more steadfastly,

though she is impossible, than he loved her alive

with the fickleness I fear and mourn.


So I would wish, O Phyllis, in your beauty,

to see you sometimes loving, sometimes aloof,

that for constancy I adore even disdain.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Flee from the sun
translations.text:
Flee from the sun: the sun flees, and life

unravels by the hands of life itself;

time, murderous to its offspring,

grazes ages like harvest through centuries.


Life is born, and with life is born

the fearful structure of the corpse.

What, then, does man fear in departure,

if the living rests on what lies dead?


What has passed is gone; the future

has not yet been lived; the present

is not, for motion is its essence.


Only what is unknown is sure:

this world, a republic of wind,

with Chance for its monarch.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: I weep, Phyllis, but without a show
translations.text:
I weep, Phyllis, but make no display;

I know how to grieve, not how to complain.

I weep toward my heart: let pain know

I weep, not the outward effort.


Though water, it does not resist

the fire I keep as treasure;

I would not weep if my dignity

did not increase it without violence.


Fire leaves my breast and returns to it,

like a clock that, as it threads the sands,

receives those same grains again.


I suspect love would lack its share

of pains against me; so it prepares

to keep its sorrows in me as in a clock.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: I shall sing of love so sweetly
translations.text:
I shall sing of love so sweetly

in the time I steal from its pain

that a heart that never felt love

will begin to confess it feels love.


It will see no happiness lasts

beneath the upper heavens,

and high or lesser joys

imitate the current here below.


It will see that no lover finds

steadfastness (though it may in torment,

adore a marble idol's beauty).


For if all love is hope,

and hope is a bond of wind,

who can love securely in constancy?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: You weep, Phyllis, because the town murmurs
translations.text:
You weep, Phyllis, because the town censures

your life, your reputation, your conduct,

and recklessly treats every sign

like a crime with biting judgment.


Your bold freedom goes so far

as to have the very vice called its sign;

you take beauty as a trade,

not as a privilege.


At times you laugh at those who slander,

not because their charges lack foundation—

your heart undeceives you of that.


You feel only their kind of guilt:

since the fruit of sin pleases you,

you laugh at those who sin for no gain.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: I believe your course and picture it
translations.text:
I believe your course and picture it,

for it leaves only traces to believe.

I saw you as one, so one life seemed spare,

swift Marquis, winged Bernardino.


In the clear air you would overtake

the arrow, make it sleep;

I looked too late as you set out—

too late, for the road came first.


Sight joins you, number divides you;

both tell the truth, though neither

shows the effects its truth foretells.


Do not let those who see you doubt;

hold another feast, to seem two,

for equals praise nothing that is one.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Though the divine ravisher of Europa
translations.text:
Though the divine ravisher of Europa

felt her disdain, he excused her:

wishing to be overcome, she fought;

some defenses show the way.


Feminine resentment lies so near

to pleasure that pleasure always wins.

The boldest woman does not wish to be cold;

she wishes to seem so, Licino.


If Philida listens and answers you,

though she seems untouched by love,

stir her hardness with gentle pleas.


Let her heart govern you in what it hides,

for what she means is not to avoid sin: she seeks

to sin, but with an excuse.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Today, Fabio, you married Lisena
translations.text:
Today, Fabio, you married Lisena,

who yesterday gave you love's sweet poisons;

in vile cups filled with venom,

Love's bee poorly arranges its honey.


I cannot promise you a calm sea,

nor that you will sound it with such a ship;

she who even made a reed grow weak

was no one to trust with a mast's risks.


You asked (and got your wish) that Hymen

purify your bed, and blameless Lisi

stand decorously beside you.


But on the very terms Orpheus had,

they give you your bride: she turned back;

Fabio, you must not look behind you.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Jacinta, that violent artificer
translations.text:
Jacinta, that violent artificer,

withholding the very water she spills,

set such flame in the deceived thirst

that crystal hides another element.


My lips do not complain of the torment

of being sent away by her who calls them;

what kindles a nobler anger is to see

that her stinginess took deliberate art.


You were born generous, and an avaricious cradle,

O luckless stream, dares make you so,

though your current makes the lip its enemy.


Even the elements are ruled by fortune.

Let water complain here of art,

if it was born a gift and dies an injury.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Your fall was not due to the bullet
translations.text:
Your fall was not due to the bullet

(for lead is unsafe against the swift);

unlocked was a harsher bolt,

leaving your second wound idle.


Dying, you are born today, chosen beast;

the arm saves you from steel.

Though the manner is mortal, life lies

not in the first birth but the better one.


Stopped between two suns and one death,

you wonder if heaven lent you mercy

to seek the swift thing or flee it.


O fortune, no lesser god in beasts!

Do not run: for one destined to be blessed,

standing still is also an act.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: The Phoenix, in barbarous fashion, applies
translations.text:
The Phoenix, in barbarous fashion, applies

flames to its end, to rise from its sunset;

to trust a new dawn to a setting sun

is noble, yet barbarous, conduct.


But Fabia, sun of Spain, devotes herself

today to your senator's wise lament,

and, phoenix more enduring, more radiant,

sacrifices her feathers in your grief.


O barbarous once more, though ingenious

eastern bird, that trusts to your end

and injury the eternity you celebrate!


O Fabia, phoenix, wise and beautiful,

who entrusts to her father's origin, in dense flame,

the eternity of her ashes!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Speaking with his lady, now dead
translations.text:
Heaven took you at your first dawn,

human flower, not dead but interrupted,

in faith that you lived here wronged

for only the instant you were human.


How early your snow—or rose—

was shaken off by the wind's rage!

How late, through your life, you taught

my hopes to learn their vanity!


If mortal prayer, the lover's voice,

can reach the land of light where you tread,

then loving what I cannot see is merit.


If you can declare your will,

know that my hope died when you did;

let my desire be known to have failed.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: A tyrant fashioned from burning bronze
translations.text:
A tyrant fashioned from burning bronze,

seeking the most dreadful insult,

made a bull whose terrible hollow shape

he watched consume the wretched offender.


So as not to pity the sufferer

or grant compassion any pardon,

he arranged that the hidden man's cries

sound like bellowing in the shining metal.


My spirit, Phyllis, shut inside

your disdain, when it reaches your ears

does not sound as my words intended;


So that my groans may not move you,

changed into the metal of your disdain,

the soul speaks, and you hear the senses.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Love’s revenge, shot in vain
translations.text:
Love's revenge was that daring, punished

fire, shot in vain, where he showed himself

more blind than god, when he trusted your hand

with the charge of your injury.


An element is man's enemy,

yet cannot unsettle a sun.

Let Love plead, not burn: only a plea

was born to conquer sovereignty.


Celia, you no longer risk harm

from fire's violence or Love's revenge,

for your snow or rigor surpasses it.


The weak are always ripe for learning;

since power is left to hope,

if Celia knows what Love cannot do—?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.
